lead: Mass transfer is easier to write once every species has its own velocity. Species A moves with velocity v<sub>A</sub>, and c<sub>A</sub> v<sub>A</sub> is its molar flux N<sub>A</sub>. That flux contains two parts: A drifting relative to the mixture, and the whole mixture moving. This chapter fixes the vocabulary of velocities, fluxes and reference frames for binary and multicomponent mixtures. It also separates molecular diffusion, the random walk of molecules, from eddy diffusion, the mixing by turbulent lumps. Every later calculation of D, absorption and distillation uses this language.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for concentration, mole fraction and the idea of a component moving because of a concentration difference.

blocks.text: Pick a small window fixed to the laboratory wall. Species i crosses it with an average velocity v<sub>i</sub>, in m/s. Its molar concentration is c<sub>i</sub>, in mol/m³. The molar flux of i through this fixed window is N<sub>i</sub> = c<sub>i</sub> v<sub>i</sub>, in mol/(m²·s). The total concentration is c = Σc<sub>i</sub>, and the mole fraction is y<sub>i</sub> = c<sub>i</sub>/c. For a binary mixture A + B, c = c<sub>A</sub> + c<sub>B</sub> and y<sub>A</sub> + y<sub>B</sub> = 1.

The molar flux N<sub>A</sub> is not the mass flux. The mass flux is n<sub>A</sub> = ρ<sub>A</sub> v<sub>A</sub> = M<sub>A</sub> N<sub>A</sub>, in kg/(m²·s). Here ρ<sub>A</sub> is the mass concentration in kg/m³ and M<sub>A</sub> is the molar mass in kg/mol. The mass fraction is w<sub>A</sub> = ρ<sub>A</sub>/ρ.

sections.h3: Molar average velocity and diffusion flux

blocks.text: The mixture itself has a velocity. The molar average velocity is u = Σc<sub>i</sub> v<sub>i</sub>/c = ΣN<sub>i</sub>/c, in m/s. For a binary, u = (N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>)/c. The diffusion velocity of A is v<sub>A</sub> − u. The diffusion flux of A is J<sub>A</sub> = c<sub>A</sub>(v<sub>A</sub> − u), in mol/(m²·s). This J<sub>A</sub> is measured relative to the molar-average frame, not the laboratory wall.

Add and subtract c<sub>A</sub> u: N<sub>A</sub> = c<sub>A</sub> v<sub>A</sub> = c<sub>A</sub> u + c<sub>A</sub>(v<sub>A</sub> − u) = y<sub>A</sub>(N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>) + J<sub>A</sub>. Rearranged, N<sub>A</sub> = J<sub>A</sub> + y<sub>A</sub>(N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>). The term y<sub>A</sub>(N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>) is the bulk flow; it is not diffusion. In a binary, J<sub>A</sub> = −J<sub>B</sub> because c<sub>A</sub>(v<sub>A</sub> − u) + c<sub>B</sub>(v<sub>B</sub> − u) = Σc<sub>i</sub> v<sub>i</sub> − c u = 0. But N<sub>A</sub> is not −N<sub>B</sub> unless the fluxes are equimolar, N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub> = 0.

blocks.where: N<sub>A</sub> and N<sub>B</sub> are fixed-frame molar fluxes in mol/(m²·s); J<sub>A</sub> is the diffusion flux of A in mol/(m²·s); y<sub>A</sub> is the mole fraction of A. The second term is the bulk flow.

blocks.text: Other frames have other names. The mass-average velocity is u<sub>m</sub> = Σρ<sub>i</sub> v<sub>i</sub>/ρ, and the mass-average diffusion flux is j<sub>A</sub> = ρ<sub>A</sub>(v<sub>A</sub> − u<sub>m</sub>). The volume-average frame uses volume-fraction weighting; it is common for liquid mixtures. Use N<sub>A</sub> in the fixed frame, J<sub>A</sub> in the molar-average frame, and j<sub>A</sub> in the mass-average frame.

Molecular diffusion comes from random molecular motion. Molecules of A and B collide and swap places even when the fluid is still. Eddy diffusion comes from turbulence. Eddies carry lumps of fluid, with their A and B, from one place to another. Eddy diffusion is fast in the core of a pipe and zero at a solid wall, where the eddy size falls to zero.

The measured mean flux can contain both parts. Write J<sub>A</sub> = J<sub>A</sub>(mol) + J<sub>A</sub>(eddy), then N<sub>A</sub> = J<sub>A</sub> + y<sub>A</sub>(N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>). The eddy part is modelled with an eddy diffusivity D<sub>E</sub>, in m²/s: J<sub>A</sub>(eddy) = −D<sub>E</sub> dc<sub>A</sub>/dz. Here dc<sub>A</sub>/dz is the gradient of the mean concentration, in mol/m⁴. D<sub>E</sub> depends on flow speed, geometry and distance from the wall; it is not a property of the A–B pair. At the wall D<sub>E</sub> → 0, so only molecular diffusion survives.

The molecular part uses D<sub>AB</sub>, the molecular diffusivity of the pair at that temperature and pressure. Chapter 1.3 gives Fick's law for that part. The topic of mass transfer coefficients turns that near-wall molecular region into a single coefficient. For a dilute species, engineers often add D<sub>AB</sub> + D<sub>E</sub> as an effective diffusivity, but the bulk term stays separate.

examples.question: A binary gas at 300 K and 1 atm has c = 40.6 mol/m³ and y<sub>A</sub> = 0.30. The measured molar fluxes are N<sub>A</sub> = 3.0×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s) and N<sub>B</sub> = 1.0×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s). Find the molar average velocity u, the diffusion flux J<sub>A</sub>, the velocity of A and its diffusion velocity.
steps: Given c = 40.6 mol/m³, y<sub>A</sub> = 0.30, N<sub>A</sub> = 3.0×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s), N<sub>B</sub> = 1.0×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s). The total molar flux is N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub> = 4.0×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s).
Molar average velocity: u = (N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>)/c = 4.0×10⁻³/40.6 = 9.85×10⁻⁵ m/s.
Concentration of A: c<sub>A</sub> = y<sub>A</sub> c = 0.30 × 40.6 = 12.18 mol/m³.
Diffusion flux: J<sub>A</sub> = N<sub>A</sub> − y<sub>A</sub>(N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>) = 3.0×10⁻³ − 0.30 × 4.0×10⁻³ = 3.0×10⁻³ − 1.2×10⁻³ = 1.8×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s).
Velocity of A: v<sub>A</sub> = N<sub>A</sub>/c<sub>A</sub> = 3.0×10⁻³/12.18 = 2.46×10⁻⁴ m/s.
Diffusion velocity: v<sub>A</sub> − u = 2.46×10⁻⁴ − 9.85×10⁻⁵ = 1.48×10⁻⁴ m/s. Check: J<sub>A</sub>/c<sub>A</sub> = 1.8×10⁻³/12.18 = 1.48×10⁻⁴ m/s.
examples.answer: u = 9.85×10⁻⁵ m/s, J<sub>A</sub> = 1.8×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s), c<sub>A</sub> = 12.18 mol/m³, v<sub>A</sub> = 2.46×10⁻⁴ m/s, and the diffusion velocity v<sub>A</sub> − u = 1.48×10⁻⁴ m/s.
examples.check:
c = 40.6
yA = 0.30
NA = 3.0e-3
NB = 1.0e-3
Ntot = NA + NB
u = Ntot / c
cA = yA * c
JA = NA - yA * Ntot
vA = NA / cA
vdiff = vA - u
print(f'{u:.2e}')
print(f'{JA:.1e}')
print(f'{cA:.2f}')
print(f'{vA:.2e}')
print(f'{vdiff:.2e}')

traps: Calling N<sub>A</sub> the diffusion flux. N<sub>A</sub> is the fixed-frame flux; J<sub>A</sub> is the diffusion flux. At large y<sub>A</sub> the bulk term y<sub>A</sub>(N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>) is a big part of N<sub>A</sub>. Setting N<sub>A</sub> = J<sub>A</sub> gives a wrong D in Chapter 1.3.
Assuming N<sub>A</sub> = −N<sub>B</sub> always. Only equimolar counter-diffusion has that; in general J<sub>A</sub> = −J<sub>B</sub> while N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub> is not zero.
Mixing units of mass and molar flux. n<sub>A</sub> = M<sub>A</sub> N<sub>A</sub>; use kg/(m²·s) for n<sub>A</sub> and mol/(m²·s) for N<sub>A</sub>.

Using the molar average velocity u as the fluid flow velocity. u is a concentration-weighted mean of species velocities; the bulk term is y<sub>A</sub>(N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>), not c<sub>A</sub> times a guessed flow.

Treating eddy diffusivity D<sub>E</sub> as a fluid property. D<sub>E</sub> depends on turbulence and position and falls to zero at a wall; D<sub>AB</sub> depends on the pair, temperature and pressure.

quiz.q: Define the molar flux N<sub>A</sub> and the diffusion flux J<sub>A</sub>. State the frame and SI unit of each.
quiz.a: N<sub>A</sub> = c<sub>A</sub> v<sub>A</sub> is the molar flux of A through the fixed laboratory frame, in mol/(m²·s). J<sub>A</sub> = c<sub>A</sub>(v<sub>A</sub> − u) is the diffusion flux relative to the molar-average frame, also in mol/(m²·s).

quiz.q: In a binary mixture, why is J<sub>A</sub> = −J<sub>B</sub> but N<sub>A</sub> usually not −N<sub>B</sub>?
quiz.a: By definition J<sub>A</sub> + J<sub>B</sub> = c<sub>A</sub>(v<sub>A</sub> − u) + c<sub>B</sub>(v<sub>B</sub> − u) = (N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>) − c u = 0, because c u = N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>. So J<sub>A</sub> = −J<sub>B</sub> always. The fixed-frame fluxes carry the bulk term as well: N<sub>A</sub> = J<sub>A</sub> + y<sub>A</sub>(N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>). N<sub>A</sub> = −N<sub>B</sub> only in the special case N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub> = 0, equimolar counter-diffusion; in the worked example N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub> = 4.0×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s), so N<sub>A</sub> ≠ −N<sub>B</sub> even though J<sub>A</sub> = −J<sub>B</sub> = 1.8×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s).

quiz.q: A binary gas has c = 50 mol/m³, y<sub>A</sub> = 0.20, N<sub>A</sub> = 4.0×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s) and N<sub>B</sub> = 1.0×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s). Find u, c<sub>A</sub>, J<sub>A</sub> and v<sub>A</sub>.
A student sets N<sub>A</sub> = J<sub>A</sub> for a concentrated binary gas. Explain the error and its effect on the diffusivity found from the next chapter.
quiz.a: N<sub>A</sub> = J<sub>A</sub> + y<sub>A</sub>(N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>). For A moving through stagnant B (N<sub>B</sub> = 0) this gives N<sub>A</sub> = J<sub>A</sub>/(1 − y<sub>A</sub>), so N<sub>A</sub> is larger than J<sub>A</sub>. If the student puts the measured N<sub>A</sub> into Fick's law as if it were J<sub>A</sub>, the diffusivity comes out too large by the factor 1/(1 − y<sub>A</sub>): 11 % too large at y<sub>A</sub> = 0.1, twice too large at y<sub>A</sub> = 0.5. The error vanishes only for a dilute A or equimolar counter-diffusion.

quiz.q: Distinguish molecular diffusion from eddy diffusion. Why does eddy diffusivity fall to zero at a solid wall?
quiz.a: Molecular diffusion is random molecular motion and exists even in a still fluid. Eddy diffusion is mixing by turbulent eddies carrying fluid lumps. At a wall the turbulent fluctuations are suppressed, so eddy size and D<sub>E</sub> fall to zero; only molecular diffusion remains.

beyond: Not for the exam. In CFD the eddy diffusivity comes from a turbulence model such as k–ε, and the turbulent mass flux is closed with a turbulent Schmidt number. Search next for turbulent Schmidt number and the Stefan–Maxwell equations.
